### Ownership and group structure

Amkor is a listed company whose votes are substantially influenced by one family. Susan Y. Kim, the Chairman, and family members and affiliates own about 49.5% of the shares and can determine or substantially influence shareholder votes and board elections; about 29.6 million of those shares, received in a 2013 note exchange, are subject to a voting agreement that requires them to be voted neutrally to the extent the family's aggregate voting holding exceeds 41.6%. For creditors the mechanism is that a leveraged recapitalization or sale needs family support and family interests are tied to the franchise, which lowers takeover risk, while payout policy is set by a family-influenced board. The parent borrows and issues the notes; the Korean and Japanese subsidiaries borrow locally, Guardian Assets, Inc. guarantees the notes and the revolver, and Amkor Technology Singapore Holding Pte. Ltd. also guarantees the revolver, so debt of the parent is structurally behind subsidiary liabilities.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_amkr_amkr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 19–21; 10-Q_2026-09-30_amkr_amkr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 36, 74–75; Business & governance (CP-1A)
### Revenue drivers and pricing power

Revenue is cyclical, concentrated and exposed to program timing, not recurring. FY2025 net sales were USD 6,707.981 million, with 29.8% from the largest customer, 11.1% from a second and 72% from the ten largest; communications fell as a share from 46% in FY2025 to 37% in the third quarter of 2026. Management describes the semiconductor industry as cyclical and lists the absence of backlog and the short-term nature of customer commitments among the factors that move results, so volume visibility beyond the advance payment agreements is limited. Pricing power is not evidenced: the gross margin gain came from a lower-material-content mix and higher utilization, not from stated price increases. The credit consequence is that a program transfer, lost design or inventory correction at one or two customers moves revenue and utilization faster than costs can adjust, while growth in computing and in automotive and industrial of 37% each in the third quarter shows where new volume is coming from.
### Cost structure and margin resilience

Margins can be defended in a growth quarter but not shown to hold under volume pressure. Materials were 50.7% of third-quarter net sales against 57.5% a year earlier, and because customers consign wafers and bear unused materials, materials behave largely as a pass-through, so the margin is set by what remains after materials. Net sales less materials rose 16.15% to USD 981.264 million while conversion costs rose 10.25%, which is operating leverage working in Amkor's favor; with a substantial fixed cost base, the same leverage reverses when volume falls. Labor was 10.1% of net sales and depreciation 8.6%, and depreciation will rise as the Arizona facility is placed in service. The implication is that EBITDA margin of 20.66% in the third quarter should be read as a favorable-mix level until a falling-volume quarter shows the floor.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_amkr_amkr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 12, 29–31; 10-K_2025-12-31_amkr_amkr-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 23; calculation K13; calculation K14
### Capital intensity and cash conversion

Cash conversion has turned from supportive to dependent on advances. Issuer-defined free cash flow was USD 359.275 million in FY2024 and USD 307.873 million in FY2025 and was negative USD 319.068 million in the first nine months of 2026; on the stricter measure of operating cash flow less capital spending the third quarter alone was negative USD 61.609 million against negative USD 306.852 million in the first half. Capital spending was 22.19% of nine-month net sales, against 13.49% in FY2025, with capital expenditure payables of USD 496.129 million still to be paid. Nothing in the filings separates maintenance from growth capital spending, so flexibility exists only on spending that is not yet contracted, while commitments of USD 1,951 million are already contracted. EBITDA converts to cash at 81.77% in the nine months on operating cash flow, but 23.01% of the operating cash flow of the last 21 months is a rise in customer advances.

### Covenants, liquidity detail and claims outside debt

The agreements governing the debt contain a minimum interest coverage ratio and a maximum consolidated leverage ratio, and management states that Amkor was in compliance at September 30, 2026 and expects to remain so for at least twelve months; no level, step-down or definition is printed, so headroom is not calculable and the leverage computed here, carrying debt over calculated EBITDA, may differ from the covenant definition. Liquidity at that date was cash and cash equivalents of USD 1,603.015 million, short-term investments of USD 773.181 million, the undrawn revolver of USD 1,000.0 million expiring in May 2030 and USD 62.1 million available under subsidiary facilities, of which the Korean facility of about USD 59 million expires in May 2027, within twelve months. USD 200.0 million of standby letters of credit are outstanding against customer advances; the filing states the full revolver as available, so they do not appear to reduce it, but the issuing facility is not stated. Claims outside the debt figure are finance lease obligations of USD 185.6 million and operating lease obligations of USD 98.5 million in future minimum payments, pension and severance obligations of USD 73.931 million, purchase obligations of USD 2,687.6 million and non-recourse receivable factoring of USD 30.4 million in nine months; management expects no material effect from legal proceedings, and none of these items is added to debt here.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_amkr_amkr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 5, 10, 18, 21, 25, 34–36; calculation K21; calculation K27
### Porter's five forces

Competitive rivalry is moderated by technical barriers at the advanced end, where flip chip, memory and wafer-level processing were 81.82% of nine-month sales, but the annual report names established providers mainly in Asia, contract foundries and electronics manufacturers offering some advanced packaging, Chinese firms building a China-for-China supply chain and customers' own in-house capabilities; mainstream wirebond products, 18.18% of sales, are where that rivalry is least cushioned by technology. New entrants face high capital needs, which is also the burden Amkor carries. Substitutes are in-house packaging by foundries and integrated device makers, which would remove volume rather than price. Buyer power is the dominant force: the ten largest customers were 72% of net sales and the largest alone 29.8%, and commitments are short, so a large customer can move programs between suppliers and sites, as the transfer from Korea to Vietnam shows; credit consequence is volatile utilization and a margin that depends on retaining a few programs. Supplier power over laminate substrates, leadframes and wire is partly neutralized because customers bear unused materials.

### PEST analysis

Policy and trade conditions are material to credit quality here, so the analysis is run. Political and regulatory factors cut both ways: the USD 407 million government award and a 35% investment tax credit support the Arizona build but are conditional, and trade restrictions, tariffs and the tension around Korea and Taiwan threaten a supply chain with 54.20% of net property, plant and equipment in Korea. Economic factors are cyclical demand and currency: the 37% growth in computing and in automotive and industrial rests on data-center and driver-assistance spending, which is cyclical, and Amkor has hedged part of its net investment in foreign subsidiaries. Technological change favors Amkor while it keeps pace in advanced packaging, which is why capital spending is rising. The credit implication is that policy support is real but conditional, and geographic concentration in Korea raises the severity of a regional disruption.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_amkr_amkr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 35, 41, 50, 61; 10-K_2025-12-31_amkr_amkr-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 62, 129; calculation K16
### SWOT analysis

Strengths: the scale and technology position in advanced packaging, low net leverage of 0.61x, 0.64x pro forma for the expected land purchase, a ladder with little due before 2030, and customers prepaying for capacity. Weaknesses: capital spending that exceeds operating cash flow, customer concentration, thin free cash flow and operating cash flow that leans on advances, and unprinted covenant levels. Opportunities that could improve credit quality: receipt of the government award and of the advances, a ramp of the Arizona facility that diversifies production geography, and growth in computing and automotive end markets. Threats that could weaken it: a loss or transfer of programs at the largest customers, a cyclical downturn while commitments are signed, trade policy and regional conflict affecting Korea, and shareholder payouts that outrun free cash flow.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_amkr_amkr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 34–37, 50; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation K01; calculation K16
### Financial profile and credit quality

Scale and market position are the clearest support: net sales of USD 7,461.269 million over the last twelve months and the position as the largest US-headquartered provider make the issuer large enough to absorb shocks. Competitive advantage rests on advanced packaging capability that customers are paying to reserve, though no contract terms are disclosed. Business diversification is mixed: end markets are spread, but customers and the Korean asset base are concentrated. Cost and capex flexibility is narrow while USD 1,951 million of construction is contracted. Margin stability is the weaker side of the earnings profile because the latest gain is mix-driven. Free cash flow stability is the weakest dimension, negative on both definitions in 2026 and flattered by advances. Refinancing and capital markets access is shown by USD 1.15 billion of convertible notes in May 2026 and USD 500.0 million of notes in September 2025, though quotes are below par. Liquidity is adequate with cash, short-term investments and the revolver exceeding stated twelve-month obligations 1.15x. Financial policy and governance is moderate: family control, continuing payouts and unprinted covenants offset the absence of documented extraction. On the broader definition that also deducts short-term investments, net debt at September 30, 2026 was USD 91.04 million against net cash of USD 546.14 million at the end of 2025, and a pro forma figure for the land purchase is not established. The trend is a strong balance sheet drifting toward heavier use of it, with key missing data in covenant terms and customer contracts.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_amkr_amkr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 4–8, 19–21, 24–25, 34–37; Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation K02; calculation K17; calculation K21; calculation K25
### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

Over the next 12 to 24 months the outlook is for rising capital spending and rising net debt, with timing set by advance receipts. Tailwinds are demand for advanced packaging in computing and automotive, customer prepayments, the ramp of the Vietnam facility, the investment tax credit and the Korean grant support of up to about USD 110 million; headwinds are the doubling of commitments, higher depreciation from new capacity, program transfers, and the cyclical risk that customers' demand falls after capacity is built. Over three to five years the first phase of the Arizona facility is expected to start manufacturing in the first half of 2028, so the payoff arrives after the spending peak and the credit depends on utilization then. Sector headwinds are tariffs, export controls and regional tension; company-specific headwinds are customer concentration and the family-influenced payout policy.
### Downside scenario

The realistic downside is a delay in customer advances or a pause in a lead customer's programs while the contracted spending continues. The first operational break would be falling utilization at plants that have a substantial fixed cost base, which turns a flat sales quarter into lower gross margin because conversion costs rose USD 57.42 million year on year. The financial transmission is lower EBITDA and operating cash flow, with the advance build ceasing to add cash; the shortfall falls first on cash and short-term investments of USD 2,376.2 million and then on the USD 1,000 million revolver. As an illustration only, if the fourth quarter repeats the third quarter's operating cash flow while capital spending reaches the USD 1.26 billion implied by guidance, the fourth-quarter free cash outflow would be USD 776.42 million, 32.67% of cash and short-term investments, and if last-twelve-month EBITDA were also 25% lower, net leverage would be about 1.55x. That would not threaten liquidity within twelve months, but a revolver draw would increase secured claims ahead of the unsecured notes and would test covenant levels that are not printed. The observable triggers are slipping advance receipts, quarterly free cash outflow above the third quarter's USD 61.609 million, a revolver draw, and sales below the year-earlier quarter. Resilience appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress over the next twelve months on the stated liquidity; the weak point is any later period in which advances do not arrive while spending stays at contracted levels, because 2027 spending and customer terms are not stated.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_amkr_amkr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 7–8, 25, 30, 34–37; 10-Q_2026-06-30_amkr_amkr-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 7; calculation K03; calculation K05; calculation K06; calculation K13
### Overall credit view

Overall, Amkor presents an adequate but concentrated business profile supported by scale, advanced packaging capability, low leverage and prepaying customers, but credit quality is constrained by a debt-funded capacity build, customer concentration and unprinted covenant levels. Cash-flow durability appears adequate and dependent on advances: EBITDA covers interest comfortably, yet free cash flow is negative on both definitions in 2026. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on delivering the Arizona facility on time and on keeping the revolver and Term A Loans, both due in May 2030, available through the build. The primary downside path is a slip in advance receipts or a loss of lead customer programs while spending of USD 1,951 million is contracted. Further analysis would require the executed credit agreement and indentures, customer advance terms, a total cost for the Arizona facility, ratings and peer figures. Fundamental credit synthesis completed. Top risk: customer-funded capacity spending that is committed before the cash arrives.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_amkr_amkr-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 21, 34–37; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation K01; calculation K03; calculation K11
